name: Space Electronics
scope: Radiation tolerance, version-locked toolchains, 20-year-old silicon, test-like-you-fly

claims.claim_text: NASA's materials and reliability research is a primary reference source for terrestrial electronics as well as spaceflight: the agency has published extensively on lead-free soldering, is one of the world's leading investigators of the tin whisker problem, and does substantial work on component reliability and radiation hardening.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, to even for important for our industry in terms of, they've done lots of soldering, research on lead-free soldering. They're one of the world leaders in researching the tin whisker problem. And other, you know, component reliability and radiation hardening and all that sort of jazz.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: Space-grade semiconductors are sold on a per-unit basis with individual test and certification records for each device, rather than being screened by lot sampling like commercial parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: Each one comes individually tested and certified as well.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: Some radiation-sensing parts sold for satellite use exist specifically to detect a nuclear detonation and assert a hardware pin when one occurs, so that the spacecraft can immediately drop into a protective low-power mode.
claims.quote_verbatim: And, um, and if you're wondering what its use is, um, it's primarily designed for, um, space, uh, satellites and things when they detect a nuclear explosion. Yeah. Then this pin goes low and I don't know, it shuts down. Yeah. You probably, you probably go into a battery save mode at that point, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: Memory in spacecraft accumulates single-event bit flips over mission duration. The Voyager spacecraft suffered a bit flip that was recovered from and attributed to a cosmic ray strike, an attribution that is inferred rather than directly measured because no cosmic ray detector was aboard to prove it.
claims.quote_verbatim: And what we observe is that if you send up a computer system with a bunch of memory in it, that over time, the bits get flipped. The Voyager spacecraft, in fact, I was just reading in the last – I don't know, within the last year, had a bit flip in it somewhere. And they were able to get things back. And then they assumed that it was a cosmic ray.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: The single-event upset rate in space is predictable rather than mysterious: irradiating memory in a beam produces a known percentage of bit flips, and multiplying that susceptibility by the measured cosmic ray density in orbit predicts the flip rate actually observed on orbit.
claims.quote_verbatim: But what we know is if you shoot cosmic rays at memory, you get a certain percentage of flips. And if you measure the density of cosmic rays in space and you predict what you think is going to happen, that's what happens.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: The classic radiation mitigation for space memory is to abandon density and use physically large storage cells, so that a bit is held by on the order of fifty thousand electrons rather than fifty, requiring a much harder particle strike to upset it.
claims.quote_verbatim: So our reaction to it for space applications mostly has been you make great, big, honking memory cells. Yeah. So that instead of, you know, 50 electrons stored on a gate somewhere, you've got, you know, 50,000 electrons stored on a gate. And so it takes a lot harder hit in order to knock that thing off balance.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: The other standard defence against radiation-induced upset is redundancy at the memory level: triplicate the memory and compare, so a single corrupted copy can be outvoted.
claims.quote_verbatim: Another strategy is you make redundant memories. You just triple them. Just have three of them.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Entry into the early United States astronaut corps required an engineering degree; Neil Armstrong and the whole of the original Mercury 7 and the Apollo astronauts were engineers, and many were also test pilots.
claims.quote_verbatim: Neil Armstrong was an engineer, as were all of the original Mercury 7 and Apollo astronauts. So were all engineers. You had to have a degree in some form of engineering to get into the space program back then.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: A CubeSat is a standardised very small satellite measuring ten centimetres on a side with a mass under one kilogram, a form factor designed so that satellites can be handled as a commodity payload.
claims.quote_verbatim: For listeners who don't know what it is, ArduSat is a CubeSat project. CubeSats are very small satellites. They're 10 centimeters on a side. They're under a kilo in mass.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: CubeSats reach orbit as secondary payloads: because launch vehicles are sized in fixed capacity increments and primary satellites are built light, spare payload capacity exists on most commercial launches, and CubeSats are packed into that leftover volume around the main payload.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they basically piggyback along as a secondary payload on some other launch. So if some commercial launch is going up with a communications satellite or whatever, because of the way – because lift vehicles are designed to have certain capacities and satellites are designed to be small and light, often there is excess payload space. So what happens is that CubeSats are packed in extra space around whatever the main payload is and taken up into orbit.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Even at CubeSat scale the economics are not hobbyist: around the early 2010s the launch alone ran roughly thirty-five to fifty thousand dollars, and the hardware being flown represented anywhere from ten thousand to a hundred thousand dollars of value going into low Earth orbit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because the thing is that even getting a CubeSat into space is an expensive exercise. The launch itself might be $35,000 to $50,000. And the platform itself, you might be up for between – it varies depending on what you're doing. But it might be $10,000 or it might be $50,000 or $100,000 worth of hardware that you are sending up into low-Earth orbit.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Spaceflight programme data is routinely lost to media attrition: the original Apollo 11 moon landing tapes and the Pioneer telemetry tapes were both lost, and even when old media is recovered, reading it back is itself a hard engineering problem. Keeping multiple physically separated copies is the only defence.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, like completely, like all the original tapes, lost, gone, you know, like it, it, it's hard enough reading the back even if you do have them, let alone, you know, yeah, just losing these things. It's nice for like when they do recover that stuff, it makes for a good story, but, uh, yeah, it'd be better if there was like triplicate copies of everything.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: The Apollo moon programme cost roughly eighty billion dollars in inflation-adjusted terms, while NASA's 1989 ninety-day study for a crewed Mars mission was costed at a minimum of four hundred and fifty billion dollars, an order-of-magnitude jump that ensured Congress never funded it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was about $80 billion adjusted, right? But this was going to be $450 billion minimum, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, System Design & NAND - Mercurial Mars Mission

claims.claim_text: The Mars Direct architecture, developed by a small task group at Martin Marietta including Robert Zubrin as a reaction to the ninety-day study, proposed a long-stay, directly-launched, repeatedly-flown Mars campaign costing fifteen to twenty percent of NASA's existing budget rather than a new multi-hundred-billion-dollar appropriation.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they formed this little task group with, this guy was in it, and they came up with an idea for what's called Mars Direct. And it's going to Mars, get in there, stay in there for a long time, get in there directly, stay in there for a long time, exploring the damn thing, and then continuously exploring it, mission after mission after mission, and do it for like 15 to 20% of the existing NASA budget.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, System Design & NAND - Mercurial Mars Mission

claims.claim_text: The Space Shuttle was only partially reusable: the orbiter returned but the boosters and external tank were effectively expended each flight, so the per-launch cost stayed enormous despite the reusable framing.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was a reusable shuttle, kind of. You know, the boosters were one off, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cheap Respins And A Time Machine - Multiscience Mercenary Marketplace

claims.claim_text: Concentrator photovoltaic cells are designed to run at very high temperatures under focusing lenses and become more efficient as they get hotter, which suits satellites and space probes but leaves them a niche technology on Earth, where they will not displace conventional rooftop panels.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, like for, there's always got to like these high temperature, uh, solar cells are designed to operate at ridiculously high temperatures. And they use lens focused lenses to actually, you know, actually the, the hotter they get, the more efficient they become.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: An Earth-imaging CubeSat constellation can be flown in a sun-synchronous ring so that the planet rotates underneath the satellites, turning the fleet into a continuous line scanner for the whole surface. This replaces the conventional model of targeted imagery, in which a satellite is commanded to point at a specific spot, with constant capture and later download.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we, um, we operate these cube sets in, in constellations. And so the idea is that, um, each satellite, uh, will be launched into, into a ring and sun singular orbit. And so we'll have, uh, depending on the, the orbit, uh, a number of satellites. And what will happen was as these satellites are orbiting, the earth is rotating underneath them and we end up getting a line scanner for the planet. And so we'll be able to, um, to capture this. And so instead of targeted imagery, which is how, um, basically all, um, imaging satellites operate right now, we'll actually just be constantly capturing and then downloading that data.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: Satellite imagery is georegistered after the fact by searching an area for known ground control points, then propagating the fit through the rest of the image strip: once one frame is matched, neighbouring frames in the line can be found and shifted until all control points are satisfied. This corrects for parallax, terrain and pointing error.
claims.quote_verbatim: So is this like if there's, if there's like angles or, uh, parallax effect, that kind of thing? Or if the, um, you know, if there's terrain or if the, the satellite wasn't pointing exactly where we thought it was, it can do this search within the area and then find it and then propagate that through this, uh, through the strip of images, knowing like a known control point, then it can easily find the next ones in the line and move them around until it's, um, satisfied the ground control points.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: CubeSats are designed to commission themselves without ground intervention: after deployment a healthy satellite detumbles, works through its commissioning sequence, establishes a stable orbit attitude and reports itself ready for commands on its own, so an operator can miss the first contact pass entirely and still find the fleet alive.
claims.quote_verbatim: And we see that the satellites have already made first contact, have already started going through their commissioning process or like de-tumbled or like in stable orbits and are like awaiting your command.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: The deployment mechanism is a real failure mode independent of the satellite: on one ISS-based launch the NanoRacks deployer did not respond to repeated deploy commands, leaving a batch of finished CubeSats stuck inside the dispenser with no recourse from the ground.
claims.quote_verbatim: And, uh, the crazy part was for our last launch, uh, which was also from the space station, uh, for the flock one B satellites, uh, there was a problem with the nano racks deployer. And so they send the deploy signal and nothing happened and they send the deploy signal and nothing happened. And so our satellites are stuck in this, um, satellite deployer.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: Launch latency, not build time, dominates the schedule of a small satellite programme. Hardware is sealed into its capsule and then waits, first on the ground, then aboard the space station until crew time is available to move it to the deployer pod, and each step adds delay outside the builder's control.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then it just sits there. And so there's still that, like, you know, we're agile, but like our, our lag time is still brutal because then we get up to the space station. We're just sitting on the space station until like the astronauts have time to then move us over to this pod and then put that pod out the window. And then once that pods out the window, they have like another, you know, it's huge lag until all the, you know, turns out that if this satellite, if this launch goes up, then we have to wait another few days.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: The board houses and machine shops that survive in high-cost regions such as the San Francisco Bay Area do so on aerospace and medical work, because only those segments carry margins high enough to absorb the local cost base.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think a lot of them for medical and for aerospace, there's still like, there's still a meaningful amount of aerospace stuff, especially. Things that have margins, basically.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Aerospace-oriented suppliers price and schedule for aerospace programmes, so a hardware startup approaching them typically finds quotes with roughly twice as many digits as expected and timelines measured in multiples of years, making them a poor fit for fast-moving small teams.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it's funny seeing them like try to engage with startups. It's like, no, this is not a, this is not a three-year project and there are like twice as many zeros on the end of that price as there possibly should be.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Microgravity aboard the International Space Station has been proposed as a manufacturing environment for ultra-precise parts, because without gravity a molten mass can form a perfectly round object; the practical obstacle is that the finished part still has to be brought back down.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're saying that now one of the best places to do that is the International Space Station. Because you can make perfectly round objects. Yeah, you don't have gravity.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: Older GPS receivers took minutes to achieve a first fix and asked the user whether the unit had moved more than about three hundred kilometres since last use, because the receiver's stored rough position and almanac had to be invalidated before it could reacquire; modern receivers lock within seconds when the previous position is still roughly valid.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, you know, like if you hop on a plane, you fly somewhere, and you turn on your GPS, it says, have you moved? You know, after a couple of minutes, it says, have you moved more than 300 kilometers since your last, you know, operation?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Nerd Calendar

claims.claim_text: A satellite launched in 1967 that failed to reach its intended orbit and lost contact began transmitting again forty-six years later, when its uncontrolled tumble happened to bring the solar panels into enough sunlight to power the transmitter and simultaneously aligned the antenna toward Earth.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's still tumbling. And it just happened to tumble in the right orientation where the solar panels got enough power. And, and it was aligned to transmit back and it started transmitting.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: World Trade Futurity (WTF)

claims.claim_text: Uploading new firmware to an on-orbit satellite is treated as one of the highest-risk operations in a mission, because a corrupted image or a single wrong bit in the transfer can leave the spacecraft unrecoverable.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it kind of made sense because they like the idea with satellites that are out in space. You know, when they update the firmware, it's a very scary nail-biting process of like, oh, boy. Put the wrong bit when you're updating firmware.
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: The European Space Agency has evaluated MicroPython for satellite use precisely to avoid reflashing firmware in orbit: with a stable interpreter core resident on the spacecraft, changing behaviour becomes a matter of uploading a new script file and running it, rather than rewriting the executable image.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they like the idea of having an interpreted language where you don't really need to change that firmware. You've got your Python core up there. But, okay, we want to change the satellite functionality a little bit.
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: The Holmdel horn's advantage over a conventional dish is very low side lobes. An ordinary parabolic antenna scatters RF off the edge of the dish and therefore sees the ground, picking up the noise temperature of the Earth, which is far warmer than space and ruins very low noise measurements.
claims.quote_verbatim: And, uh, it has the advantage that it has very, very low side lobes. So, uh, most parabolic antennas have this problem in that they, they, the RF scatters off the edge of the dish and you can see the ground. Uh, so they end up receiving some of the noise temperature of, of earth, which is a lot warmer than space.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: The Holmdel horn antenna, a parabolic reflector integrated into a horn, was built for the passive Echo satellite experiment and paired with a liquid-helium-cooled maser as its low noise amplifier, an early example of cryogenic front-end design for space communications.
claims.quote_verbatim: And so the, the Holmdell horn, uh, was built to avoid that problem. And they actually used a liquid helium cooled maser as a low noise amplifier, which is fascinating.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: At satellite production volumes, unit cost effectively drops out of the design trade space: one flown payload processor module had a total production run of five boards, so per-unit component and fabrication cost was irrelevant next to reliability and schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: And when you're dealing with that sort of project, basically, cost is meaningless. You really don't care. So we made a total of five boards.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer
claims.episode_title: An(other) Interview with Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: A standard practice on small satellite programmes is to build a functional replica of the flight article and keep it at the operations site, so that code changes and commands can be tested against an exact copy of the flying hardware before being uploaded to the real spacecraft.
claims.quote_verbatim: Two of them were to go in the actual satellites. And one was in a functional satellite replica, which was set up at the headquarters so that they could run tests on it before actually uploading code to the real satellites.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer
claims.episode_title: An(other) Interview with Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: The commercial case for CubeSat constellations rests on their short life: the satellites cannot maintain orbit, so they decay and burn up after roughly five years, and the operator refreshes the whole fleet with current-generation hardware rather than flying twenty-year-old silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think that's the, the main like upside they're selling investors is like these things just go up. They last for five years and you can completely refresh the.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Amateur satellite organisations historically obtained launches for free or at token cost as goodwill payloads. Once CubeSats standardised the small-payload market and commercial providers began selling ride share slots, that goodwill capacity was priced, and a slot that had been free came to cost on the order of three hundred thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: They used to get launches basically for free or super low cost. And then once CubeSats came around and people like SpaceX came around and actually kind of changed the whole paradigm of the launch industry, they really couldn't compete. Because now for what they got for free now costs like $300,000.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: The AMSAT Fox series began as 1U CubeSats providing a standard reusable bus, comprising the battery system, RF chain and computing, into which university groups could drop experimental electronics; the bus provides the data downlink and the experimenters supply only the payload.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I guess the best way to say the Fox series and its evolution is it started off in 1U CubeSats, like literal cubes. And its main point was to develop like the backbone of battery system, RF system, computing, the ability to put your experimental electronics and tests on it from universities. And the universities do their experiments in space.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: Most amateur radio satellites operate as a bent pipe: a signal transmitted up on one frequency is retransmitted in real time back down on another, with no onboard processing. The practical effect is that a handheld transceiver is given an antenna a couple of hundred miles high, extending its range from a town to a large fraction of a continent.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the way that most CubeSats today, most amateur radio satellites work today is just what you call a bent pipe. So you transmit on one frequency up to the satellite and it retransmits you in real time down to Earth. So the effect of that is having is like you transmit up to the CubeSat and it makes you look like you're a couple hundred miles above the sky.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: A high-altitude balloon payload was protected against condensation by coating the assembled boards completely in clear nail polish as an improvised conformal coating. The reasoning was that the boards would be chilled hard at altitude and would then descend into humid summer air, where water would condense directly onto cold copper.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, um, we actually did things like we, we didn't know about conformal coat at the time, but we, we actually took like clear nail polish and like completely coated the boards. Cause we figured, well, condensation is going to form this board cause it's going to get really cold at altitude. And then when it falls back down, um, it's going to hit the humid atmosphere of, you know, Rochester, New York summer.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: That improvised coating worked as intended: the payload fell through a thunderstorm and was recovered with visible globs of water sitting on the microcontrollers, and the electronics were still running.
claims.quote_verbatim: And in retrospect, when we opened it up, it was, it was literally, it was still on blinking. And there was like globs of water on like some of the, like the MSP 430s.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: What aerospace recruiters looked for in a student flight project was not the result but the reasoning: conformal coating the boards, designing for the environment, and being explicit about which requirements were mandatory versus which were nice to have.
claims.quote_verbatim: And when we were showing this to SpaceX recruiters, uh, when they came to RIT, they just basically latched on and realized a lot of that forward thinking. Oh, like conformal coding boards, designing for reliability and like knowing what your requirements were. Like pictures are nice to have, but it must work.
claims.speaker: Brent And Bryce Salmi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: The commercial small-satellite sector inverted the aerospace career ladder. In traditional large aerospace it can be a decade before a design reaches orbit, and a given seniority may be required before an engineer touches flight hardware at all; at a fast-moving launch company an engineer in their early twenties can have a board of their own design deployed on satellites.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like, um, you know, I think, uh, Brent can also attest to like some of the stuff we worked on, but like, you know, uh, you look at other companies in bigger aerospace and it could be a decade before the hardware gets in orbit or, you know, you might have to be, you know, a certain seniority to even work on flight harder. Like, like circuit board with my name on it in my design, you know, deployed satellites when I was 24.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: Satellite attitude control is normally done without expending propellant: reaction wheels are spun up inside the spacecraft, and conservation of angular momentum rotates the satellite in the opposite sense.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, they use gyrators. If people don't know how they orbit satellites and they don't use, like, rocket vector thrusters, you know, they actually use gyroscopic wheels and they spin them up. And the inertia of the wheel makes the satellite spin.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Secret Buzzer Handshake

claims.claim_text: Reaction wheels are a recognised wear-out item. A batch of satellites launched together suffered a common-mode failure in which their wheels began to stick and gum up roughly a year into the mission.
claims.quote_verbatim: And he was talking about how all these gyroscopic wheels in these satellites were failing. You know, they sent up a whole bunch of satellites and they all started, like, a year later or something, they all started to, like, all the wheels in them started to gum up and stick and stuff like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Secret Buzzer Handshake

claims.claim_text: European small satellite builders can use ESA's ESTEC test facilities in Noordwijk, including a very large anechoic chamber, essentially free of charge. A CubeSat-class satellite was characterised there to measure how its multiple antennas couple to and interfere with one another at RF, a test few small companies could otherwise afford.
claims.quote_verbatim: And so we went to ESA and we, because we were already working with them and they had, you know, they have a huge anechoic chamber. It's, it's probably, it's the biggest I've ever seen. So we put a little tiny dinky satellite in there to, to test it, but it was all, you know, basically free of charge because we have, um, uh, access to all that, all that, uh, all these, all those facilities in the Netherlands.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Maarten Engelen

claims.claim_text: The DARPA chip-scale atomic clock found its market wherever a stratum-three frequency reference is needed without the volume pricing of a conventional standard, and a unit was flown as an experiment on the International Space Station.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're showing up in any place where you need a stratum three clock and don't want to pay a whole lot of volume for it. It's flying in the International Space Station, which we almost burned down.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom Lee

claims.claim_text: Dedicated small launch vehicles are sized around a payload of roughly one hundred and sixty-five to four hundred and fifty pounds, a mass that corresponds to a satellite rather than a crewed capsule; the vehicles are around thirteen metres tall against roughly eighty metres for a heavy lifter.
claims.quote_verbatim: And so they're targeting for those who plan long at home, they're targeting 165 to 450 pound payload. So that's, you know, that's like, that's not a human person.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Optimization Beast

claims.claim_text: A laser-linked satellite constellation can beat terrestrial fibre on long-haul latency because light travels appreciably faster through free space than through glass; simulations of the Starlink network suggest a New York to Seattle link could take roughly half the time of the current fibre route.
claims.quote_verbatim: Uh, they wrote in, uh, the, the difference in timing is because fiber is going through glass, which is like much, much lower speed than going through, through free space.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Optimization Beast

claims.claim_text: The Starlink constellation was planned at a scale of roughly two and a half to five thousand satellites, and at least two other operators announced systems of comparable size, changing the density of low Earth orbit by orders of magnitude within a few years.
claims.quote_verbatim: And that's like 2,500 to 5,000 satellites or something like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Optimization Beast

claims.claim_text: Power, not silicon area, sets the architecture of a planetary CubeSat instrument. With a total instrument power budget of perhaps fifty watts, only one to two watts may be available to compute a four to eight thousand point FFT behind a six gigasample per second ADC, which rules out FPGAs and forces custom silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you have to think about the power requirements too. If you do a planetary mission to another planet or something on a CubeSat or a SmallSat or something, which is what we're all talking about now, you know, your instrument power budget might only be 50 watts, which means, you know, forget the FPGAs and stuff. You've got basically a watt to two watts to compute that FFT at six gigahertz clock.
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: High-value prototype boards are powered up for the first time under a two-person rule: a second engineer independently verifies the bench supply settings before the board is connected, because a single slip on a hundred-thousand-dollar assembly is unrecoverable.
claims.quote_verbatim: They don't let just, you know, Joe Schmoe just go hook it up to the lab power supply. No, you know, no, you've got to have, it's a two person rule for valuable boards like this. You've got to have somebody double check your settings on the power supply.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Two Person Rule

claims.claim_text: Triple modular redundancy, or TMR, runs three copies of a computation and votes on the result. It works against radiation-induced upsets because the probability of two or three independent copies faulting in exactly the same way is vanishingly small; a divergent three-way result is treated as everyone being wrong rather than a winner being picked.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then the idea is that statistically the likelihood of the two are going to fault the exact same way is almost infinitesimally small.
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: A radiation-tolerant computer is qualified up a ladder of increasingly expensive environments: radiation chambers on the ground first, then high-altitude balloon flights, then sounding rockets that go up and come back down, and only then an orbital demonstration.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we started building circuitry and we, we started putting it in like a radiation chambers and then we started flying it on high altitude balloons. And we got some opportunities to, uh, to put them on a sounding rockets, which are the, the rockets that just go up and come back down.
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: After a year-long experiment aboard the International Space Station in 2017, the same radiation-tolerant computer was flown in two loaf-of-bread-sized CubeSats, RadSat-U and RadSat-G, which return operating data on each pass over a ground station so that upset behaviour can be measured on orbit rather than inferred.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they're, they're called cube sats and they're like about the size of a loaf of bread. And so we put the computer in these two little satellites and they're actually orbiting earth right now. Uh, so they, they pass over ground stations and we, we get data from it to see how the computer's operating.
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: CubeSat material selection is constrained by reentry rather than by orbit: a satellite built of a dense refractory metal such as tungsten would survive reentry and reach the ground, and would not be approved. Aluminium, FR-4 and standard solder ablate in the upper atmosphere and disperse as particles.
claims.quote_verbatim: I couldn't, you couldn't get a cube sat approved that was made of tungsten, uh, cause it would land. And so, but if you're just using aluminum and, you know, FR four and, and standard solder, that stuff just burns up and it just lives in the upper atmosphere as particles.
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brock LaMeres

claims.claim_text: Large aerospace firms sit on Mentor Graphics or Cadence rather than mid-market EDA tools, and the very largest, such as Boeing, run all of them at once because different divisions were acquired as separate companies and kept their own toolchains.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's either mentor graphics or cadence. Actually aerospace is kind of a unique area where if you're talking like Boeing, they literally use like all of them. It just depends on the division.
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: A 3U CubeSat is a stack of three 10-centimetre cubes, 10 by 10 by 30 centimetres in the stowed configuration, with antennas and solar panels that deploy after release so that the on-orbit envelope is larger than the launch envelope.
claims.quote_verbatim: So so I basically did all of the electrical integration and some of the mechanical integration. And since it's a satellite is pretty small, it's it's called three U and when you is a cube of 10 by 10 by 10 centimeters. So our satellite is like 10 by 10 by 30. And then it has a bunch of deployable antennas and deployable solar panels.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: The power chain of a small satellite comprises maximum power point trackers for the solar panels, a battery charger and battery, and a power distribution stage that also monitors the loads and protects against latch-up, a radiation-induced failure mode that can destroy the spacecraft if power is not cycled quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then, of course, you have your your maximum point power trackers for your solar panels. You have a battery charger, the battery, you have some some power distribution that also does monitoring and protection against latch ups or other weird things that can happen that could damage your spacecraft.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: There is nothing exotic in most small satellite electronics; the effort goes into reliability, because the hardware cannot be touched after launch and is built in ones or handfuls. A ten percent unit failure rate that would be acceptable in a consumer product means losing the mission.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just usually a lot of time and effort has gone and making it reliable as you can't really poke at it anymore after after you launch it. And you usually only have one or a handful. So it's not like if 10 percent of my my units dies, I'm still happy.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: A CubeSat that deploys but never transmits telemetry is not necessarily dead: operators have used a large dish to listen for the harmonics radiated by the microcontroller crystals aboard the spacecraft, which is enough to establish whether the processors are running at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if I've actually heard some crazy stories of like cube sets that were deployed and that didn't send back telemetry, but you can still get like a giant scope dish and then listen for the crystals on your, on your, uh, on your microcontrollers to see if they're running or not.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Small satellites are built in batches, and at least one complete flight-identical unit is retained on the ground after launch so that anomalies can be reproduced and fixes rehearsed against real hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: Uh, depends a little bit. Usually you build them in batches and then you at least want to have one sort of clone that you keep on the ground after, after they launched.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: The de facto mechanical and electrical standard in the CubeSat world has long been the PC/104-derived stack, with mounting holes on an irregular 87.24 millimetre pattern and a large 54-pin through-header. The header makes an assembled stack effectively impossible to separate again without damage.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then it has this, this giant 54 pin header, which makes it impossible to take units apart after, if you've put them together. Uh, so that, that's been sort of the standard in, in CubeSat world for, I don't know, since it started.
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: CubeSat modules are pitched at around eleven millimetres per board in the stack, which has to accommodate the inter-board connectors and any taller components, so the usable component height on each board is a hard mechanical budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, so, so our modules are, I think 11 millimeters is the standard thickness and you definitely need some space for, for connectors and, and, you know, some, some parts that are slightly higher profile.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: When a satellite builder migrates off the legacy PC/104 stack to its own backplane, the practical route is a legacy interface board that bridges the remaining PC/104-format modules onto the new bus, rather than redesigning every subsystem at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we still have a couple of boards that are, uh, they're still using that, that PC 104 form factor. And then we basically have a, a legacy interface board that connects those to our bus.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Spacecraft software is verified by exhaustive simulation rather than by field testing, because there is only one article and no opportunity to iterate: every retry protocol, every RF condition and every scenario expected on orbit has to be exercised in a model before flight.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because they just have to simulate every single scenario. They have to get every single, like, you know, all the retry protocols, all of their RF stuff, every scenario that they expect to see in space. They can, they don't get to send, you know, they don't get to send more than one thing, so they have to simulate it.
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Aerospace and defence measurement practice sits at the top of the calibration hierarchy: instruments are run against daily calibrations and every variation is recorded, because an out-of-tolerance measurement on a satellite or radar is only discovered once the hardware is dead junk in orbit. Cell infrastructure tolerates more, handsets more again, and amateur equipment is calibrated only as far as the user needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the aerospace defense guys, you know, people making satellites and making radars, they're like at the top tier of everything has to be in calibrated. You have to run your daily calibrations. You have to record any variation.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore
claims.episode_title: Microwave measurement with Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Publishing even the existence of amateur rocket work attracts proliferation interest: a New Zealand builder who put up a website merely demonstrating that a cruise missile could be built by an individual received offers of large sums from correspondents in Iran and Pakistan for the plans, which he referred to his national security service.
claims.quote_verbatim: Not showing how to do it, but just highlighting the fact that this could be done. And I was starting to get emails from some very interesting places, from Iran, from Pakistan, and people offering me large amounts of money for the plans to my missile.
claims.speaker: Bruce Simson
claims.episode_title: Missle Man with Bruce Simson

claims.claim_text: Product lifecycle management tooling is a known weak point even at well-resourced hardware companies: SpaceX built its own PLM system because nothing available on the market was adequate, and established enterprise firms with unlimited procurement budgets manage hardware data in spreadsheets because legacy PLM products were built for process rather than for speed during new product introduction.
claims.quote_verbatim: And he was an early mechanical engineer at SpaceX and he confided that they had the same problems. Like it's, and, and then was now a well-known anecdote that, you know, SpaceX built their own PLM system because they were so frustrated with what was available in the market.
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Old space describes the 1960s to 1980s programme model: top-down design, waterfall development, and layered chains of subcontractors beneath a prime. New space is defined against it by tolerating different part specifications and much faster iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, I mean, it's certainly not an official term of any kind, but people who work in new space, I think probably sort of differentiate it from old space. Sorry. So it's the difference between maybe like, say if you're taking the extremes, like a sixties or seventies, or even just like eighties, like NASA approach, like kind of a top down design, really using basically.
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Radiation-hardened parts carry extreme prices for old silicon: a twenty-year-old CPLD listed on a general distributor at three thousand dollars is priced that way because it has been radiation hardened and put through pre-testing and characterisation, not because of the die.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I always think about like rad hard parts, you know, you see them on like a DigiKey or Mauser and you're like, Oh, why is that part? Why is that, you know, 20 year old CPLD costs $3,000. And it's because it's rad rad radiation hardened or whatever.
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: CubeSat sizes are expressed in units, where one U is a 10 by 10 by 10 centimetre cube; larger spacecraft are built as integer multiples such as 3U, giving a family of standard envelopes rather than bespoke geometry.
claims.quote_verbatim: So a cube sat is basically a 10 by 10 by 10 centimeter unit. A cube sat might just be that one unit, or you might have a three by one or there's different configurations of these things.
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Because CubeSats are small, launch pricing and manifesting are driven by mass rather than by the volume constraint of the form factor.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there's, there's some amount of volume constraint, but because cube sats are pretty small, it's, uh, any launched orbit, you're really talking about mass is the thing you care about.
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Passive component miniaturisation lags in flight hardware: a satellite builder asking for a 0201 flight-qualified capacitor is ahead of what the industry supplies, and 0402 is the realistic practical minimum size for spacecraft use.
claims.quote_verbatim: And we were dealing with a satellite company looking to do an 0201 flight cap. So they're not yet at that point as an industry. But I'd say 0402 would be the realistic spacecraft limit.
claims.episode_title: Capacitor Schoopage with Ron Demcko from AVX

claims.claim_text: The original NASA spacesuits carried no closed refrigeration cycle. Cooling came from venting compressed refrigerant into the vacuum of space, using the expansion into the low-pressure environment to chill the reservoir, with a circulator distributing the cooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: Actually, interestingly, uh, I think in the original NASA spacesuits, they were not using a refrigeration system. Oh, really? They were just using compressed refrigerant, which they were just like venting into space.
claims.speaker: Amitabh Shrivastava
claims.episode_title: Refrigerators and Robots with Amitabh Shrivastava

claims.claim_text: At companies where a software defect is unrecoverable, engineers inspect the compiler's output and check it against expectation for anything that looks wrong; this was routine practice on flight software, and is not warranted for the overwhelming majority of designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: The same way that like, you know, at SpaceX, people did look at the compiled output and like, you know, sniff it for anything that doesn't look right. Of course, you know, but for like 99% of designs, that's not the case.
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko
claims.episode_title: Intelligent Routing with Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors price flight-qualified parts against the value of the mission rather than the cost of the silicon, because a single failure destroys a payload worth billions and the part has to survive on orbit for many years.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, look at this, you know, SpaceX, they send a $5 billion shuttelite and it blows up, right? Right. So, you know, there's a lot of money that's going into it and, you know, we get our pound of flesh.
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: An internal budget audit of the Artemis programme found it so far behind schedule and over budget that further allocations to Boeing and the other contractors were withheld, with the second vehicle the specific trigger.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they did an audit of the whole program and found that it's so far behind schedule and so over budget that they wouldn't authorize any more money to go to Boeing or any other contractors. It's like a whole slew of contractors to Artemis. But they were so late with the second rocket and they're so over budget that they weren't going to allocate any more money.
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: The Space Launch System is a fully expendable vehicle costing on the order of four and a half billion dollars per flight, which is difficult to justify commercially against a fully reusable competitor. Its architecture is essentially a mid-1970s launch system built decades later.
claims.quote_verbatim: The thing is, if SpaceX gets their launch approval, new license for Starship, it would be very hard to sell the idea of a rocket that's like $4.5 billion a shot, completely disposable, against Starship, which is going to be completely reusable. It just... It's like, you know, the problem is that the Space Launch System, it's a great rocket for 1974.
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Contrary to public perception, the large majority of NASA's project portfolio is aeronautical research such as jet engines, wing configurations and aircraft design, even though the majority of the money goes to heavy-lift launch programmes.
claims.quote_verbatim: So NASA has a laundry list of things it wants to do with planetary exploration, vehicles, research. And people think that all NASA does is launch big rockets, whereas, like, you know, 80% of what NASA does is aeronautical research, you know.
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: NASA's programme structure is set by Congress, which both selects the mission and attaches the constraint that contractors in every funding state must participate. The resulting geographically distributed contractor architecture is a principal cause of the schedule and cost overruns that are later attributed to the agency itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: And here's the kicker. You've got to use contractors in every single one of our states.
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: A crewed Mars architecture assembled by internal consensus at NASA became unaffordable because every department insisted its own idea be included, producing a scheme so convoluted and expensive that Congress rejected it outright. Design by internal stakeholder accommodation is a recognised failure mode for large programmes.
claims.quote_verbatim: And because every department of NASA, every person said, oh, we want our idea to be included. So, NASA bent over backwards so that it was such a convoluted scheme for going to Mars that, you know.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Buying a commercial off-the-shelf satellite subsystem such as a power and battery module does not eliminate the work; the effort shifts to integrating that subsystem with the flight computer and the rest of the spacecraft, which is why some CubeSat companies choose full in-house design instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can. Again, you end up spending a lot of time integrating that with your flight computer and the rest of the system.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: A fully vertically integrated CubeSat builder makes solar panels from bare cells mounted onto PCBs, plus solar regulators and maximum power point trackers, flight computers, UHF radios, and the complete attitude determination and control system of star trackers, reaction wheels, magnetorquers and sensors.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we, you know, we build everything from, we take cells, we put them onto PCBs, we build solar panels, solar regulators, maximum PowerPoint trackers, flight computers, UHF radios, the whole ADCS system, which consists of star trackers, reaction wheels, magnetalkers, sensors, everything is all designed in-house.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: Cleanliness requirements on a small satellite are imposed partly by the launch service provider rather than by the payload: the spacecraft must be visibly clean before the launch provider will accept it onto the vehicle, independent of any contamination sensitivity of the instrument itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the cleanliness is driven by two things. There's a requirement for it to be visibly clean for the launch service provider.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: Rideshare access to orbit is brokered: a launch service provider aggregates many 6U CubeSats into its own dispensers, ships those dispensers to the launch company for integration, and one Transporter-class mission can carry over a hundred separate space objects manifested by many different companies.
claims.quote_verbatim: So what they do is they take a whole bunch of 6U CubeSats and they have dispensers for them. And then they'll put our CubeSat into their dispenser and then they'll ship that to SpaceX to integrate on the transport or any of the ride share missions that SpaceX have. So there was over 100 different space objects on that one transport mission.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: Small satellites in the current market span roughly one hundred to five hundred kilograms, sitting between CubeSats and traditional large spacecraft.
claims.quote_verbatim: So small sats was kind of like 100 to 500 kilo spacecraft.
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: Falling launch prices push operators up the mass curve: a builder moving from a 25-kilogram CubeSat-class platform to a 250-kilogram spacecraft bus does so because the launch cost no longer punishes the extra mass, and the larger bus buys larger optics.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're currently building our next spacecraft bus, which is, you know, Astralis, which is a, you know, 250-kilo class spacecraft. So going from sort of 25 kilos up to 250 kilos.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: The RP2040 and RP2350 microcontrollers turn out to be unusually radiation resistant because they carry no on-chip flash and boot from external memory, removing the floating-gate storage that is normally the most radiation-sensitive structure on a microcontroller die.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it turns out that 2350 and 2040 are actually very radiation resistant because we don't use on-chip flash. 2350 boots from external flash.
claims.speaker: Chris Boris
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Pairing a flash-less microcontroller with an MRAM or mask ROM boot device yields a radiation-resistant processor system from commercial parts, because MRAM stores state magnetically and is itself extremely radiation resistant.
claims.quote_verbatim: And MRAM happens to be extremely radiation resistant as well. So if you pair an MRAM chip with or a mast ROM with a 2350, you actually end up with a pretty cool radiation resistant processor system.
claims.speaker: Chris Boris
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Early customers took commercial RP2350 parts, ran their own radiation testing, and concluded the devices were suitable to fly, an example of a mainstream consumer microcontroller being qualified for orbit by its users rather than by the vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it turns out that some early customers of 2350 took their parts and did some radiation testing on them. And it turns out that they're very suitable to fly.
claims.speaker: Chris Boris
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Simulation-first development has compressed satellite schedules to the point where concept to orbit inside one year is achievable for a small spacecraft, rather than the multi-year cycles of traditional aerospace.
claims.quote_verbatim: We have this great customer at Aerospace with whom we've been working kind of in a really rapid development project where, you know, from concept to orbit below one year.
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Launch scheduling is no longer the dominant risk for a standard small payload: a rideshare slip on a commercial launch is now typically measured in a month, not the years that a builder had to plan around historically.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there was this like little glitch somewhere last summer, but, but it was a delay of one month. Right. So it isn't so bad these days if you're launching something fairly standard.
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Building satellite software on portable abstractions such as Zephyr, and validating it in a simulator such as Renode, means a mid-project change of flight hardware does not invalidate the software effort, because the underlying interfaces stay the same.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the fact that the things we're using are portable, both Zephyr and Renaud, et cetera. It's like, okay, we're changing hardware now because reasons, but that's okay because the underlying abstractions are the same.
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Commercial space before the 2010s meant a small number of large primes such as Boeing and Maxar building large satellites and launch vehicles, with slow design cycles and comparatively few spacecraft in orbit; the current density of on-orbit hardware is a recent change.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like, Boeing or Maxar or companies that built large satellites and or large launch vehicles. Design cycles were relatively slow. The number of spacecraft in orbit was relatively low compared to today.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Propellant efficiency compounds in spacecraft design because the propellant itself has to be launched. A thruster three times as efficient does not merely save mass at liftoff, it buys three times as much manoeuvring for the same tankage.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, so the reason why it's beneficial to, to use less propellant, uh, is yeah, you have to carry it there in the first place. And once you were there, you know, if you're three times as efficient, you can do three times as much maneuvering.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: A common use of onboard thrusters is orbit raising after separation: a rideshare payload is dropped in whatever orbit suits the primary mission, and the satellite manoeuvres itself from there to its intended orbit. Station keeping against atmospheric drag in low Earth orbit similarly determines mission lifetime.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you get dropped off by a rocket in some orbit. It's not quite where you want to go. Uh, and so you use your thrusters to get to where you actually want to be.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: The customers for electric propulsion are bus integrators, the companies that assemble complete satellites, rather than the end users of the data those satellites produce.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the people who buy Hall effect thrusters or electric propulsion in general are usually people who make spacecraft. Um, so, so what we would, you know, in my business, uh, you would call them a bus integrator, um, or a bus manufacturer. And that just means people who make or put together satellites.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Constellation operators split on make versus buy for propulsion: SpaceX builds its own argon Hall effect thrusters and flies one on every Starlink satellite, Amazon's Kuiper is building its own thruster system, and most other operators buy from specialist suppliers.
claims.quote_verbatim: So like some people make their own, um, SpaceX famously makes their own Hall effect thrusters. Um, they, they build an Argon thruster, uh, and all the star links have one and they, they build it. Most other companies, I think, uh, Kuiper, which is Amazon's constellation is in theory building their own thruster system.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Xenon is the traditional Hall effect thruster propellant and remains excellent on pure performance; a switch to zinc is not a performance improvement but a supply chain and manufacturability decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like Xenon, the, the, you know, the, the traditional propellant, like Xenon is, is traditional Hall Effect thruster propellant. It's an amazing propellant. Zinc is not quote unquote better in many ways.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Zinc as a Hall effect thruster propellant is solid, so it packs more densely than any gas, cannot leak, and costs about four dollars a kilogram.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's solid, which means you can pack it more densely than any dumb gas. It cannot leak and it costs $4 a kilogram.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Choosing a solid propellant eliminates a whole class of supply chain risk: no precision orifices, no clean room gas handling, and no valves rated for four thousand PSI noble gases that are made by a single vendor on eighteen-month lead times and are contended for by semiconductor fabs.
claims.quote_verbatim: Uh, and so it's like, so it's like all of a sudden your supply chain doesn't involve like stupid, like orifices and clean rooms and like valves that are made for 4,000 PSI noble gases that take 18 months to get.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Space mechanisms use specialist lubricants formulated for vacuum, because any volatile constituent in a conventional lubricant evaporates away in orbit and leaves the actuator dry.
claims.quote_verbatim: They specialise in just lubricants for space satellites and gear and stuff, you know, because you have actuators that move and stuff. Yeah, if you have, like, any kind of, like, water element in it, it's going to, like, evaporate away, I'm sure.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

claims.claim_text: Access to orbit has moved from relationship-based contracting through large primes such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin to self-service booking: a payload slot can now be reserved from a web page with a deposit of a few thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: You go, I had to go through the Lockheed Martins and the, yeah, the rest of them. And now it's like, no, I can literally go on a webpage right now and book a slot on the next SpaceX flight. I can put it in my shopping cart, put down my $5,000 deposit and I'm on a bloody SpaceX flight.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

claims.claim_text: Gallium nitride is intrinsically close to immune to radiation damage because of its material properties, which allowed a power semiconductor vendor to build radiation-hardened GaN transistors and integrated circuits that are now widely designed into new satellites.
claims.quote_verbatim: Um, and I recognized that gallium nitrate had some unique properties that would make it virtually impervious to radiation. So we developed a bunch of radiation, hard stuff. And now we have radiation, hard transistors, the radiation, hard ICs, and, you know, all the new satellites are using it.
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: SpaceX manufactures Starlink user terminals in what is described as the largest PCB assembly plant in the United States, an example of a space programme pulling high-volume electronics assembly back onshore.
claims.quote_verbatim: They, they manufacture the Starling terminals in the, in the US's biggest PCB assembly factory.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hyper Growth and OpenClaw Interns

claims.claim_text: A satellite service that targets devices already in the field has to close its link budget against whatever antenna those devices already have, typically an omnidirectional PCB trace antenna at around fifty percent efficiency. Any requirement that the customer modify existing hardware is treated as fatal to the product, so the difficulty is deliberately loaded onto the space segment instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: So all of that is a long, um, you know, prelude into, we didn't want to have our customers change anything about their hardware. Cause we felt as soon as they had to change anything about their hardware, uh, you know, we were basically dead in the water. So your standard PCB trace, omni directional, and you know, 50% efficiency antenna.
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: Before commercial rideshare, reaching orbit meant buying a dedicated rocket, an investment on the order of a hundred million dollars once the satellite had to be built large enough to justify the vehicle. That threshold restricted spaceflight to governments and a few extremely well-capitalised private ventures.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like, you know, prior to SpaceX, you had to buy your own dedicated rocket. You're talking about probably a hundred million dollars worth of investment, both from the rocket perspective, but also building, building a satellite that justified, you know, a big enough rocket to, or like using the space efficiently.
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: A satellite startup founded in 2021 put its first three spacecraft in orbit in 2024 on a SpaceX rideshare, roughly two and a half years and under twenty million dollars from company formation to hardware on orbit.
claims.quote_verbatim: Uh, and, you know, with Hubble, it took us two and a half years and sub $20 million and we got three satellites up.
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: The characteristic failure of a small satellite is silent and terminal: some spacecraft never establish first contact after deployment, and there is no way to send anything up to diagnose them, so the hardware becomes an expensive object that eventually deorbits and burns up.
claims.quote_verbatim: Once that happens, you can't send a probe up there to talk to the satellite. Yeah. So you, you just create, you know, very expensive space rocks that eventually deorbit and burn up.
claims.speaker: Alex Haro
claims.episode_title: Space Age Bluetooth with Alex Haro

claims.claim_text: Satellite connectivity splits into distinct market segments by ground segment complexity. A broadband constellation aimed at internet service needs a phased array ground terminal, which suits gateway and premises installations but not a low-power sensor left in a field, so broadband capacity does not automatically serve satellite IoT.
claims.quote_verbatim: But I think they're currently really focusing on providing actual internet. So high bandwidth. And so you're mostly looking at more gateway type applications since their ground setup is a bit more complicated than ours.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts
